tldr: Headlines across all 20 countries converge almost uniformly on the UAE's official 'terrorist act' classification of the Flydubai cockpit attack — a rare consensus including Chinese state media, Russian state agencies, and pan-Arab outlets on an Israel-linked incident. A strong secondary track on the co-pilot's prior Oman flying ban runs through US, Israeli, Indian, and Nigerian headlines, while a parallel hero-pilot narrative ('fighting for my life', 'I could not let all those people die') runs through Anglo, Indian, and East African press.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only outlet to initially headline the incident as a 'pilots brawl', uniquely minimizing the attack as a personal altercation before later updating to the UAE's terrorism classification.

Both headlines avoid 'terrorist': the first uses 'death-dive and pilot stabbing', the second reports 'FlyDubai suspends Israel flights' — in contrast to co-Russian outlet TASS, which headlined the UAE attorney-general's official terrorism classification.

Only outlet to call the attacker a 'Terrorist' unqualified in a headline, in visceral first-person framing ('Blood-Soaked Pilot Reveals Moment He Knew He Had To Get Up Or Terrorist Would Win') that stands apart from every other outlet's more distanced language.

Only outlet to redirect the aviation-terrorism story into a domestic Hindu-nationalist culture-war headline, speculating on how 'leftists' and 'racists' would have blamed India had the plane crashed — unique among all 43 outlets in the corpus.

Only outlet to run a celebrity-tribute headline (Shah Rukh Khan, Salman Khan) for the pilot, illustrating the story's crossover into Indian popular culture in a way no other country's press replicated.

Only outlet to surface the co-pilot's social media posts on gender ('Mixed-gender workplaces ruin women') as a standalone headline, adding an ideological texture to the attacker's profile absent from all wire-driven and Western coverage.

Only outlet to headline a direct 9/11 comparison — 'Netanyahu says FlyDubai pilots prevented a 9/11 disaster' — a framing choice that dramatically scales the incident's historical resonance in a way no other outlet matched at the headline level.

bottom_line: Headline coverage presents an almost universal terrorism frame endorsed by official UAE language — including Chinese state media CGTN, Russian state agency TASS, and pan-Arab Al Jazeera — while the co-pilot's prior Oman flying ban runs as the second-most-repeated headline angle across political divides, shifting the story's advertised emphasis from 'what happened' to 'how it was allowed to happen.'
